cases.title: Constructed given name with a two-syllable surname
cases.why: A rare surname plus a constructed given name: four syllables with no lexical anchor at all.

cases.title: Constructed full name with 님께서
cases.why: A constructed full name followed by 님께서; layered honorifics after an unseen name.

cases.title: Constructed full name with 씨
cases.why: A constructed full name followed by the honorific 씨.

cases.title: Common surname with a constructed foreign-style given name
cases.why: A foreign-style given name (아델) attached to a Korean surname; transliterated given names are less frequent than native ones.

cases.title: Common surname with a rare given name
cases.why: 도하 is also the name of a city; combined with a surname it is a rare but valid given name.

ambiguity.note: Following a surname and taking the subject marker, 도하 is a given name, though it is also a city name.

cases.title: Constructed given name followed by ㅋㅋ
cases.why: A constructed given name attached to chat laughter; two unusual features together.

cases.title: Common surname with a constructed given name
cases.why: The given name is constructed with an unusual syllable (쥬) so no name list contains it; the surname alone anchors the PERSON reading.

cases.title: Constructed given name beginning with a vowel syllable
cases.why: Constructed name 라엘; tests a name that does not follow any common Korean given-name pattern.

cases.title: Common surname with a constructed given name containing 뤼
cases.why: The syllable 뤼 never occurs in native Korean given names, so the given name is constructed.

cases.title: Common surname with a constructed three-syllable given name
cases.why: A constructed given name with loanword-style syllables, making a four-syllable full name with a common surname.

cases.title: Common surname with a rare native-looking given name
cases.why: 솔뫼 combines native-looking syllables and is rare as a given name (it is also a place name), so little frequency support exists; the surname anchors the PERSON reading.

cases.title: Constructed given name in a vocative
cases.why: A constructed given name with the vocative 아; unseen name plus a suffix that must be excluded.

cases.title: Constructed single-syllable given name used alone
cases.why: A single-syllable given name with a vocative; the shortest possible unseen name shape.

cases.title: Constructed full name before the copula 입니다
cases.why: A constructed full name directly followed by the polite copula, as in a self-introduction.

cases.title: Constructed name in a form field
cases.why: A form field with a constructed name and no particle.

cases.title: Constructed two-syllable name with a loanword-style given syllable
cases.why: A short constructed name whose given syllable (젠) is a transliteration-style syllable rather than a native given-name syllable.

cases.title: Foreign full name transliterated into Hangul
cases.why: A non-Korean full name written in Hangul with a space. The name is a person but follows no Korean surname/given structure.

cases.title: Foreign given name transliterated into Hangul
cases.why: A single-token transliterated name; the Hangul spelling is the only cue and the token is also an ordinary-looking syllable sequence.

cases.title: Hanja-written rare name followed by a Hangul particle
cases.why: A hanja full name with a rare surname followed by a Hangul particle; the script boundary is the span end.

cases.title: Rare two-syllable surname written in hanja
cases.why: A two-character hanja surname plus a one-character given name, followed by a Hangul particle.

cases.title: Rare surname 빈 that is also a common syllable
cases.why: 빈 means 'empty' as a syllable and is a rare surname; the full name is a person even though the first syllable has a common lexical reading.

cases.title: Rare surname 빈 with the title 부장님
cases.why: A rare surname with a job title; 빈 ('empty') is a common syllable otherwise.

ambiguity.note: A job title with honorific particle 께서 requires a person.

cases.title: Rare surname 봉 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 봉 is a rare surname and a common syllable (봉투 'envelope'); the full name is a person.

cases.title: Very rare one-syllable surname 어
cases.why: A real but uncommon surname written with a single common-looking syllable; without a surname list, 어재윤 is easily read as a common word plus a given name.

cases.title: Rare surname 어 alone with 씨
cases.why: 어 is a rare surname and a very common syllable (어디, 어제); the honorific after it gives the only person cue.

ambiguity.note: The honorific 씨 attaches to a person reference, not to a bare syllable such as the 어 of 어디 or 어제.

cases.title: Rare surname 갈 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 갈 is a rare surname and a common syllable in words like 갈등 ('conflict').

cases.title: Rare surname 견 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 견 is a rare surname and a syllable in 견학 ('field trip').

cases.title: Hangul rare-surname name inside an English sentence
cases.why: A Hangul full name with a rare surname inside English text; both script and rarity are unusual.
cases.text: The invoice was approved by 탁서진 yesterday.

cases.title: Rare-surname names in a comma list
cases.why: Three rare-surname full names in a list; each must be found with no frequent-name support.

cases.title: Rare-surname name inside a quotation
cases.why: A rare-surname full name inside quotation marks with a quotative marker; the rare surname gives no lexical anchor and the quotes add boundary work.

projections_excluded.reason: The projection wraps the text in another pair of quotation marks, which would nest with the quotes this case is about and change what it tests.

cases.title: Rare surname 맹 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 맹 is a rare surname and a syllable inside words like 맹렬 ('fierce').

cases.title: Rare surname 옥 with a common given name
cases.why: 옥 is a real but infrequent surname and also means 'jade'; the full name must still be read as a person.

cases.title: Rare surname 팽 as the head of a new role
cases.why: A rare surname in a subject position with a promotion predicate; checks that rarity alone does not push a detector to PERSON-negative.

cases.title: Rare surname 팽 with 선생님
cases.why: A very rare surname with the teacher honorific.

cases.title: Rare surname 피 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 피 ('blood') is a rare surname and an everyday noun; the name reading comes only from context.

cases.title: Less common surname 설 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 설 is a less common surname and the word for the Lunar New Year; a calendar reading competes.

cases.title: Rare surname 탁 with a common-looking given name
cases.why: Rare surname plus a given name that is common in other combinations; tests that a rare first syllable does not cancel the name reading.

cases.title: Rare surname 탁 alone with 씨
cases.why: A very rare surname alone followed by the honorific 씨; with no given name, the rare syllable and the honorific are the only evidence.

ambiguity.note: A single syllable followed by 씨 is a surname reference, though 탁 is also an onomatopoeic adverb (thud).

cases.title: Rare-surname full name with 대리
cases.why: A rare-surname full name followed by a job title; the title is excluded.

cases.title: Rare surname 육 followed by a common given name
cases.why: 육 is a rare surname and the Sino-Korean numeral six; both lexical readings compete with the surname.

cases.title: Rare two-syllable surname 사공 with a given name
cases.why: 사공 ('boatman') is a rare two-syllable surname and an ordinary noun for a ferryman; the full name is four syllables.

ambiguity.note: The following given name and subject marker mark a four-syllable personal name.

cases.title: Romanized rare surname Dokgo
cases.why: A romanized rare two-syllable surname; the first token resembles no English word.

ambiguity.note: After the rare surname Dokgo the hyphenated given name and the approving verb mark a person; 'Young' could otherwise be an English adjective.

cases.title: Romanized very short rare surname Eo
cases.why: A two-letter romanized surname with no English counterpart; very little orthographic evidence.

cases.title: Romanized two-syllable surname Hwangbo
cases.why: Another romanized two-syllable surname that has no English lexical cue and is unfamiliar in English text.

cases.title: Romanized rare-surname name in parentheses
cases.why: A romanized rare-surname name in a parenthesis after a role word.

cases.title: Romanized two-syllable surname Namgung
cases.why: The rare two-syllable surname in romanized form: the surname is two syllables merged into one token, followed by a hyphenated given name.

cases.title: Romanized surname Seonwoo
cases.why: A romanized two-syllable surname that is also a rare given-name form.
cases.text: Seonwoo Jin-a presented the final slides.

cases.title: Romanized rare surname after a title
cases.why: A romanized rare surname after the title Prof.; the title is excluded.
cases.text: Prof. Tak Seo-jin gave the lecture.

cases.title: Transliterated Arabic given name in Hangul
cases.why: A single-token transliterated name that looks like a common noun sequence in Hangul.

cases.title: Transliterated English full name in Hangul
cases.why: A transliterated English given name plus surname; neither token follows Korean naming patterns.

cases.title: Transliterated Slavic full name in Hangul
cases.why: A transliterated foreign full name with a space, rare in Korean text, with an unfamiliar syllable sequence.

cases.title: Transliterated foreign name with the object marker
cases.why: A transliterated foreign name followed by 를 in an object position.

cases.title: Transliterated foreign names in a list
cases.why: A list of transliterated foreign names, which share no Korean naming structure.

cases.title: Transliterated foreign given name with 한테
cases.why: A transliterated foreign given name with the colloquial dative.
